Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

For a smooth manifold $M^n$, with boundary allowed, the **density bundle** is $DM=\coprod_{p\in M}D(T_pM)$. In coordinates $x$, let $|dx|=|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ be the density taking value one on the coordinate frame. On overlaps,
$$|dy|=|\det D_x y|\,|dx|.$$
A smooth density is a section with smooth real coefficient in these frames. Its support is the closure of its nonzero locus. The absolute determinants are positive smooth transition functions and satisfy the cocycle identities by the chain rule. A countable atlas and [[thm-vector-bundle-construction-from-a-smooth-cocycle]] therefore give a smooth line bundle. For boundary charts the same gluing proof uses half-space product charts; smoothness of transitions follows from their local extensions, and Hausdorffness and second countability follow as for the supplied cocycle construction. The fibers are lines by [[prop-one-densities-form-a-one-dimensional-vector-space]]. When $n=0$ the empty frame trivializes $DM=M\times\mathbb R$.

Fix $n\ge1$ and $a\in\mathbb R^n$. A real analytic germ at $a$ is an equivalence class of real functions agreeing on a neighborhood of $a$, represented on some polydisc $|x_i-a_i|<r_i$, $r_i>0$, by an absolutely convergent series $f(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N^n}c_\alpha(x-a)^\alpha$ with real coefficients. Here $0\in\mathbb N$, $\alpha!=\prod_i\alpha_i!$, and $c_\alpha=D^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$. A vector germ has a finite positive number of such components, with a common polydisc obtained by taking coordinatewise minima of their radii.

The multi-index convention and absolute convergence are those of [[def-multivariable-power-series]]; for $n=1$ this agrees with [[def-real-analytic-function]]. The same coefficients define the complexification. Indeed choose a positive real polyradius $s<r$; absolute convergence at $a+s$ bounds $|c_\alpha|s^\alpha$ uniformly. [[thm-power-series-define-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables]] therefore gives a holomorphic sum on the complex $s$-polydisc and the displayed derivative formula. Restriction to the real slice recovers $f$.

Fix $m\ge1$ and read $\mathbb C^m$ through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]]. A **multi-index** is
$\alpha\in\mathbb N^m$, with $|\alpha|=\sum_{k<m}\alpha_k$ and
$\alpha!=\prod_{k<m}\alpha_k!$ as in
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], every index running
over $k<m$ from $0$. For $w\in\mathbb C^m$ the **complex monomial** is

$$w^\alpha:=\prod_{k<m}w_k^{\alpha_k},$$

a finite product in the multiplicative commutative monoid of $\mathbb C$
([[def-monoid-finite-product]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) of natural powers
in $\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-integer-powers]]); for the zero multi-index
$w^0=1$.

**Enumerating the index set.** $\mathbb N$ is countable and
[[lem-finite-powers-of-countable-sets-are-countable]] makes $\mathbb N^m$ at
most countable; it is infinite, so there is a bijection
$\sigma:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^m$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]],
[[def-countable]]).

Let $c:\mathbb N^m\to\mathbb C$ and $a,z\in\mathbb C^m$. The **multi-indexed
power series** $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ **converges absolutely at $z$**
when the complex series $\sum_n c_{\sigma(n)}(z-a)^{\sigma(n)}$ converges
absolutely ([[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]) for one
bijection $\sigma$, equivalently for every one. The two conditions agree, and the
sums agree, because for bijections $\sigma,\tau$ the series along $\tau$ is a
rearrangement of the series along $\sigma$: applying
[[thm-absolute-convergence-of-complex-series]] to the nonnegative series of
moduli transfers convergence, and applying it again to the series itself
transfers the sum. That common value is written $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$
and no other notion of unordered sum is introduced.

**Box partial sums.** For $N\in\mathbb N$ put
$B_N:=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N^m:\alpha_k\le N\ \text{for every }k<m\}$, a finite
set, and let $S_N(z):=\sum_{\alpha\in B_N}c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ be the
corresponding finite sum ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). If the
series converges absolutely at $z$ with sum $S$, then $S_N(z)\to S$. Given
$\varepsilon>0$, absolute convergence supplies $n_0$ with
$\sum_{n\ge n_0}|c_{\sigma(n)}(z-a)^{\sigma(n)}|<\varepsilon$ and
$\bigl|\sum_{n<n_0}c_{\sigma(n)}(z-a)^{\sigma(n)}-S\bigr|\le\varepsilon$; taking
$N$ large enough that $B_N$ contains $\sigma(0),\dots,\sigma(n_0-1)$, every index
of $B_N$ outside that finite list is $\sigma(n)$ for some $n\ge n_0$, so
$|S_N(z)-S|\le2\varepsilon$. The same argument bounds $|S_N(z)|$ and the tail of
the series by the corresponding tails of the series of moduli.

The series **converges absolutely and uniformly on a set $S\subseteq\mathbb C^m$**
when there are reals $M_\alpha\ge0$ with
$|c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha|\le M_\alpha$ for every $z\in S$ and every $\alpha$, and
with $\sum_n M_{\sigma(n)}$ convergent. By
[[thm-weierstrass-m-test-for-complex-function-series]] the partial sums along
$\sigma$ then converge uniformly on $S$
([[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]]) and the series converges
absolutely at every point of $S$.

citations.quote: Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$, and $n!$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion, with the natural exponents interpreted by Integer powers $a^m$. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in Directional derivatives and partial derivatives of a map $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n$.

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $n\ge1$. For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, its **support** is
$$\operatorname{supp}f:=\overline{\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)\ne0\}}.$$
The function is **compactly supported** if $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compact.

A compactly supported $f$ is **compactly supported Riemann integrable** if there is a nondegenerate closed rectangle $Q$ with $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq\operatorname{int}Q$ such that $f|_Q$ is Riemann integrable. Its integral over Euclidean space is defined by
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f:=\int_Qf.$$
The value is independent of $Q$ by [[lem-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-is-well-defined]]. When the support is empty, $f=0$ and the value is $0$.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

derivations.claim: If $K=\varnothing$, set $\chi_N=0$ for all $N$; the empty set is a neighborhood of $K$, so every assertion is vacuous. Assume henceforth $K\ne\varnothing$. For each $x\in K$, choose concentric balls $B_{r_x}(x)\Subset B_{R_x}(x)\Subset U$. By [F1], take $b_x\in C_c^\infty(B_{R_x}(x))$ with $0\le b_x\le1$ and $b_x=1$ on $B_{r_x}(x)$. Compactness gives a finite subcover $B_{r_1}(x_1),\ldots,B_{r_m}(x_m)$ of $K$. The smooth function $ g=1-\prod_{j=1}^m(1-b_{x_j}) $ satisfies $0\le g\le1$, equals one on the open set $O=\bigcup_{j=1}^m B_{r_j}(x_j)$ containing $K$, and has compact support $S\Subset U$. This construction uses only finite subcover compactness.

Choose a nonnegative smooth bump $\rho_0$ supported in the unit ball and equal to one on the ball of radius $1/2$, using [F1]. Its compactly supported integral is finite by [F3] and positive because it equals one on a ball. Normalize $\rho=\rho_0/\int\rho_0$, so $\int\rho=1$, $\rho\ge0$, and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subset\overline B_1(0)$. Since $K\Subset O$ and $S\Subset U$, choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than one third of each distance $\operatorname{dist}(K,O^c)$ and $\operatorname{dist}(S,U^c)$.

For each $N\ge1$, put $\delta=\varepsilon/N$, $\rho_\delta(x)=\delta^{-n}\rho(x/\delta)$, and recursively $\eta_1=\rho_\delta$, $\eta_{j+1}=\eta_j*\rho_\delta$ for $1\le j<N$. Compact-rectangle Fubini [F4] and change of variables give $\int\eta_N=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\eta_N\subset\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$; [F4] also permits reassociation of these compact convolution integrals. Define $\chi_N=g*\eta_N$. The integral defining $\chi_N$ is over a fixed compact rectangle. Differentiating the smooth kernel under this compact integral is justified by uniform convergence of its difference quotients on that rectangle, so $\chi_N$ is smooth. Positivity and unit mass give $0\le\chi_N\le1$. If $\operatorname{dist}(x,K)<\varepsilon$, then every $y\in\operatorname{supp}\eta_N$ satisfies $\operatorname{dist}(x-y,K)<2\varepsilon<\operatorname{dist}(K,O^c)$, hence $g(x-y)=1$ and $\chi_N(x)=1$. Also $\operatorname{supp}\chi_N\subset S+\overline B_\varepsilon(0)\Subset U$.

For smooth compactly supported $f,h$, write $\|h\|_1=\int_{\mathbb R^n}|h|$. Fubini on a rectangle containing their supports and the triangle inequality give $ \|f*h\|_{1}\le\int\!\!\int |f(x-y)||h(y)|\,dy\,dx =\|f\|_{1}\|h\|_{1}. $ Also $\partial_j(f*h)=(\partial_j f)*h=f*(\partial_jh)$ by differentiating under the compact integral and integration by parts; there is no boundary term because the factors have compact support. For $k=|\alpha|\le N$, distribute the $k$ coordinate derivatives to $k$ distinct convolution factors in $\eta_N$. Scaling gives $ \|\partial_j\rho_\delta\|_{1}=\delta^{-1}\|\partial_j\rho\|_{1}, $ so repeated use of the preceding inequality yields $ \|\partial^\alpha\eta_N\|_{1}\le (AN)^k,\qquad A=\varepsilon^{-1}\max\bigl(1,\max_j\|\partial_j\rho\|_{1}\bigr). $ For $k=0$ this is $\|\eta_N\|_{1}=1$.

Since $\|g\|_\infty\le1$, $ |\partial^\alpha\chi_N(x)| =|g*(\partial^\alpha\eta_N)(x)| \le \|g\|_\infty\|\partial^\alpha\eta_N\|_{1} \le (AN)^{|\alpha|}. $ Thus the lemma holds with $C=1$ (or any larger fixed constant), uniformly for every $|\alpha|\le N$. The cutoffs are smooth and no analytic bump is used.

and no other notion of unordered sum is introduced.

**Box partial sums.** For $N\in\mathbb N$ put
$B_N:=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N^m:\alpha_k\le N\ \text{for every }k<m\}$, a finite
set, and let $S_N(z):=\sum_{\alpha\in B_N}c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ be the
corresponding finite sum ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). If the
series converges absolutely at $z$ with sum $S$, then $S_N(z)\to S$. Given
$\varepsilon>0$, absolute convergence supplies $n_0$ with
$\sum_{n\ge n_0}|c_{\sigma(n)}(z-a)^{\sigma(n)}|<\varepsilon$ and
$\bigl|\sum_{n<n_0}c_{\sigma(n)}(z-a)^{\sigma(n)}-S\bigr|\le\varepsilon$; taking

$|S_N(z)-S|\le2\varepsilon$. The same argument bounds $|S_N(z)|$ and the tail of

The series **converges absolutely and uniformly on a set $S\subseteq\mathbb C^m$**
when there are reals $M_\alpha\ge0$ with

with $\sum_n M_{\sigma(n)}$ convergent. By

([[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]]) and the series converges

Fix $m\ge1$, $a\in\mathbb C^m$, a polyradius $r$, a real $M\ge0$ and

$$|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}\qquad\text{for every multi-index }\alpha.$$

2. $g$ is holomorphic on $\Delta_r(a)$, with

   and every iterated complex partial derivative

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb C^m$ be
holomorphic, and let $a\in U$. If $\det J_{\mathbb C}F(a)\ne0$, then there are
open neighbourhoods $U_0\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $V_0$ of $F(a)$ such that
$F|_{U_0}:U_0\to V_0$ is biholomorphic.

If $G:V_0\to U_0$ denotes the inverse, then

$$DG(w)=DF(G(w))^{-1}\qquad(w\in V_0).$$

Let $m \ge 1$, let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}^m$ be a nonempty connected open set,
and let $f : U \to \mathbb{C}$ be holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). If there is a
nonempty open set $W \subseteq U$ such that $f(z) = 0$ for every $z \in W$, then
$f \equiv 0$ on $U$.

the hypothesis is a nonempty **open** set of zeros. An accumulation point of the
zero set is neither assumed nor sufficient in several variables; the companion
page records that stronger one-variable statement as false here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, and suppose $Dg(x)$ is invertible for every $x\in U$. Let $K\subseteq U$ be compact and Jordan measurable. For a bounded function $f:g(K)\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is Riemann integrable on $g(K)$;
2. $x\mapsto f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|$ is Riemann integrable on $K$.

When either condition holds,
$$\int_{g(K)}f(y)\,dy=\int_K f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|\,dx.$$

Precisely, if $f:D\to[0,\infty)$ is locally Riemann integrable and $(K_j)$ is a compact Jordan exhaustion, then

$$\int_D f=\sup_{j\in\mathbb N}\int_{K_j}f.$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

derivations.claim: Set $t=z_1-\psi(z')$. Taylor's formula in $t$, with the linear term zero, gives $ \phi(\psi(z')+t,z')=\phi(\psi(z'),z')+t^2a(t,z'),\quad a(t,z')=\int_0^1(1-s)\partial_{z_1}^2\phi(\psi(z')+st,z')\,ds. $ The integral is holomorphic by locally uniform convergence of the power series [F2]; $a(0, 0)=H_{11}/2\ne0$. Shrink the polydisc so $a=a(0, 0)(1+b)$ with $|b|<1$. The binomial series for $(1+b)^{1/2}$ converges absolutely by [F2], so $w_1=t\sqrt{2a(t, z')}$ is holomorphic and has nonzero $t$-derivative at $0$.

By [F4], $(t, z')\mapsto(w_1, z')$ is biholomorphic near $0$, and the phase becomes $\phi(\psi(z'), z')+w_1^2/2$. The Hessian of the reduced phase in $z'$ is the Schur complement $H_{22}-H_{21}H_{11}^{-1}H_{12}$. It is invertible because the block determinant formula gives $\det H=H_{11}\det(H_{22}-H_{21}H_{11}^{-1}H_{12})$.

For real symmetric positive-definite $H$, [F8] gives $H=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal. Since $H$ is real, $\overline L$ is another such factorization; uniqueness in [F8] gives $L=\overline L$, so $L$ is real and $H=LL^T$. On each ball $B_R$, the map $x\mapsto L^Tx$ sends a compact Jordan set to a compact Jordan set; [F11] changes variables by $|\det L|^{-1}$. Letting $R\to\infty$ and using [F12] gives the corresponding nonnegative improper-integral equality. Since $\det L>0$, [F9]–[F10] give $\det H=(\det L)^2$. Repeated compact-rectangle Fubini [F15] factors the standard Gaussian integral on $[-R, R]^n$ into one-dimensional integrals, and [F12] lets $R\to\infty$. By [F13] and the substitution $t=x/\sqrt2$ in [F14], each one-dimensional integral of $e^{-x^2/2}$ is $\sqrt{2\pi}$. Finally, $z=\sqrt\lambda w$ scales the integral by $\lambda^{-n/2}$, proving the formula for real positive-definite $H$ with the positive determinant root.

Repeating steps 1.1–2.1 on the reduced phase proves the normal form by induction on $n$, with the constant phase as the $n=0$ case. Because $\Psi$ is the composite from the original coordinates, differentiating $\phi(z)=\phi(0)+\frac12\Psi(z)^T\Psi(z)$ twice at $0$ gives the original Hessian identity $H=(D\Psi(0))^TD\Psi(0)$; taking determinants gives the asserted square relation. For a continuous parameter family, continuity of $\det H$ lets one restrict to a neighborhood whose determinant image lies in a disc avoiding zero, where a square-root branch can be fixed from its base value.

For complex symmetric $H$ with positive-definite real part, the Gaussian integral is holomorphic in its entries: on each compact subset of this matrix domain, the integrand and its entry derivatives are bounded by a polynomial times $e^{-c|x|^2}$ for some $c>0$, so [F6] permits differentiation under the integral. This domain is convex, hence connected, and $\det H\ne0$ there because $Hv=0$ would imply $\operatorname{Re}(v^*Hv)=v^*(\operatorname{Re}H)v>0$ for $v\ne0$. For $H_t=I+t(H-I)$, [F16] and determinant multiplicativity give $\frac{d}{dt}\det H_t=(\det H_t)\operatorname{tr}(H_t^{-1}(H-I))$. Thus $ L(H)=\int_0^1\operatorname{tr}(H_t^{-1}(H-I))\,dt $ depends holomorphically on $H$, satisfies $e^{L(H)}=\det H$, and is zero at $I$. When $H$ is real positive definite, its segment $H_t$ is real positive definite, so $L(H)$ is real and the branch $e^{L(H)/2}$ is positive. The real Gaussian formula from step 3.2 and the complex integral formula agree on a real open set of positive-definite matrices. In a polydisc centered at any point of that set, apply the one-variable identity theorem successively in the independent entries of a complex symmetric matrix; then [F5] extends the identity from that polydisc to the connected matrix domain.

The holomorphic $n$-form in the statement is closed: in complex coordinates its exterior derivative has repeated holomorphic differentials and no antiholomorphic coefficients. By [F7], its integral is the boundary integral on the truncation of that chain; the stated decay makes this term tend to zero as the truncation expands. Therefore the contour integrals agree.

\phi(z)=\phi(0)+\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^n w_j^2.

Its linear part satisfies $(\det D\Psi(0))^2=\det H$. For a continuous parameter family of invertible Hessians $H(p)$, near any fixed parameter $p_0$ the determinant remains in a disc avoiding $0$; choosing one square root at $p_0$ therefore fixes a continuous branch on that neighborhood. derivations.claim: Choose $r>0$ so that $\chi_N=1$ on $B_{2r}(0)$ for every $N$, the phase and amplitude are holomorphic near $\overline B_{2r}(0)$, and the stated positivity holds. The positive-phase hypothesis and compactness of $\operatorname{supp}a\setminus B_r(0)$ give $\operatorname{Im}(\Phi-\Phi_0)\ge d>0$ there. Since $a$ is bounded and $\chi_N$ is bounded by one, the absolute value of that contribution after multiplication by $e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}$ is at most $\|a\|_\infty |U|e^{-\lambda d}$, uniformly in $N$. Thus only the integral over the fixed local ball affects the power series; the complement contributes $O(e^{-d\lambda})$.

Put $\phi=-i(\Phi-\Phi_0)$, so $\operatorname{Re}\phi=\operatorname{Im}(\Phi-\Phi_0)$ and $\phi''(0)=H$. Apply [F1] to obtain a holomorphic Morse coordinate $w=\Psi(x)$ with $\phi(x)=\tfrac12 w\cdot w$. The transformed real ball is a local contour $\Gamma$ through $0$. The transformed amplitude $ b(w)=a(\Psi^{-1}(w))\det D\Psi^{-1}(w) $ is holomorphic in a fixed polydisc and has coefficients bounded by $M R^{-|\alpha|}$ for some $M,R>0$ by [F3]–[F5].

Differentiating the Morse identity in [F1] twice at $0$ gives $A^TA=H$, where $A=D\Psi(0)$. Taylor's formula gives $\operatorname{Re}(\phi(tv))=\tfrac12t^2v^T(\operatorname{Re}H)v+o(t^2)$; comparing with $\operatorname{Re}\phi(tv)\ge ct^2|v|^2$ and dividing by $t^2/2$ as $t\to0$ yields $v^T(\operatorname{Re}H)v\ge2c|v|^2$. For a real vector $v$, write $Av=u+iw$ with $u,w\in\mathbb R^n$. Then $|u|^2-|w|^2=\operatorname{Re}(v^THv)>0$ when $v\ne0$. In particular, the real projection on $A\mathbb R^n$ is injective, hence bijective by dimension, and $A\mathbb R^n=\{u+iKu:u\in\mathbb R^n\}$ for a real linear map $K$. For nonzero $u$, applying the strict inequality to $v=A^{-1}(u+iKu)$ gives $|Ku|<|u|$; compactness of the unit sphere gives $\|K\|<1$. The real inverse theorem [F6] makes the nonlinear contour $\Gamma$ a graph $u+i(Ku+r(u))$, with $r(u)=O(|u|^2)$. For sufficiently small $r_0$, the homotopy graphs $u+i(Ku+t r(u))$ remain in the holomorphic chart and satisfy $\operatorname{Re}(w\cdot w)\ge c_0|u|^2$ for $|u|\le r_0$, because the linear margin $|u|^2-|Ku|^2\ge(1-\|K\|^2)|u|^2$ dominates the $O(|u|^3)$ error. The homotopy $u+i tKu$, $0\le t\le1$, also has $\operatorname{Re}(w\cdot w)=|u|^2-t^2|Ku|^2\ge(1-\|K\|^2)|u|^2$. On the fixed outer boundary these bounds, together with boundedness of the transformed amplitude and Jacobian, make the integrals $O(e^{-c_1\lambda})$. [F7] and the contour statement in [F1] therefore deform $\Gamma$ to the real Gaussian contour, with only that exponential boundary term.

Truncate the Taylor series after total degrees below $2N$. Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

Fix $n\ge1$ and $a\in\mathbb R^n$. A real analytic germ at $a$ is an equivalence class of real functions agreeing on a neighborhood of $a$, represented on some polydisc $|x_i-a_i|<r_i$, $r_i>0$, by an absolutely convergent series $f(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N^n}c_\alpha(x-a)^\alpha$ with real coefficients. Here $0\in\mathbb N$, $\alpha!=\prod_i\alpha_i!$, and $c_\alpha=D^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$. A vector germ has a finite positive number of such components, with a common polydisc obtained by taking coordinatewise minima of their radii.

The multi-index convention and absolute convergence are those of [[def-multivariable-power-series]]; for $n=1$ this agrees with [[def-real-analytic-function]]. The same coefficients define the complexification. Indeed choose a positive real polyradius $s<r$; absolute convergence at $a+s$ bounds $|c_\alpha|s^\alpha$ uniformly. [[thm-power-series-define-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables]] therefore gives a holomorphic sum on the complex $s$-polydisc and the displayed derivative formula. Restriction to the real slice recovers $f$.

Fix $m\ge1$ and read $\mathbb C^m$ through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]]. A **multi-index** is
$\alpha\in\mathbb N^m$, with $|\alpha|=\sum_{k<m}\alpha_k$ and
$\alpha!=\prod_{k<m}\alpha_k!$ as in
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], every index running
over $k<m$ from $0$. For $w\in\mathbb C^m$ the **complex monomial** is

$$w^\alpha:=\prod_{k<m}w_k^{\alpha_k},$$

a finite product in the multiplicative commutative monoid of $\mathbb C$
([[def-monoid-finite-product]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) of natural powers
in $\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-integer-powers]]); for the zero multi-index
$w^0=1$.

**Enumerating the index set.** $\mathbb N$ is countable and
[[lem-finite-powers-of-countable-sets-are-countable]] makes $\mathbb N^m$ at
most countable; it is infinite, so there is a bijection
$\sigma:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^m$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]],
[[def-countable]]).

Let $c:\mathbb N^m\to\mathbb C$ and $a,z\in\mathbb C^m$. The **multi-indexed
power series** $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ **converges absolutely at $z$**
when the complex series $\sum_n c_{\sigma(n)}(z-a)^{\sigma(n)}$ converges
absolutely ([[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]) for one
bijection $\sigma$, equivalently for every one. The two conditions agree, and the
sums agree, because for bijections $\sigma,\tau$ the series along $\tau$ is a
rearrangement of the series along $\sigma$: applying
[[thm-absolute-convergence-of-complex-series]] to the nonnegative series of
moduli transfers convergence, and applying it again to the series itself
transfers the sum. That common value is written $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$
and no other notion of unordered sum is introduced.

**Box partial sums.** For $N\in\mathbb N$ put
$B_N:=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N^m:\alpha_k\le N\ \text{for every }k<m\}$, a finite
set, and let $S_N(z):=\sum_{\alpha\in B_N}c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ be the
corresponding finite sum ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). If the
series converges absolutely at $z$ with sum $S$, then $S_N(z)\to S$. Given
$\varepsilon>0$, absolute convergence supplies $n_0$ with
$\sum_{n\ge n_0}|c_{\sigma(n)}(z-a)^{\sigma(n)}|<\varepsilon$ and
$\bigl|\sum_{n<n_0}c_{\sigma(n)}(z-a)^{\sigma(n)}-S\bigr|\le\varepsilon$; taking
$N$ large enough that $B_N$ contains $\sigma(0),\dots,\sigma(n_0-1)$, every index
of $B_N$ outside that finite list is $\sigma(n)$ for some $n\ge n_0$, so
$|S_N(z)-S|\le2\varepsilon$. The same argument bounds $|S_N(z)|$ and the tail of
the series by the corresponding tails of the series of moduli.

The series **converges absolutely and uniformly on a set $S\subseteq\mathbb C^m$**
when there are reals $M_\alpha\ge0$ with
$|c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha|\le M_\alpha$ for every $z\in S$ and every $\alpha$, and
with $\sum_n M_{\sigma(n)}$ convergent. By
[[thm-weierstrass-m-test-for-complex-function-series]] the partial sums along
$\sigma$ then converge uniformly on $S$
([[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]]) and the series converges
absolutely at every point of $S$.

A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

An analytic double fibration is a diagram of real-analytic manifolds and real-analytic submersions
$$
G\xleftarrow{\ \pi_G\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi_X\ }X
$$
such that $Z$ is embedded in $G\times X$, both projections are submersions, and
$$
\dim G+\dim X>\dim Z>\dim G\ge\dim X.
$$
Write $C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}$ for the incidence cotangent relation. Assume $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. Let $\omega_Z$ be a nowhere vanishing real-analytic smooth density on $Z$ and let $\kappa\colon Z\to\mathbb C$ be real analytic and nowhere zero. For a compactly supported distribution $u$ on $X$, the weighted transform is the distributional density
$$
Ru=(\pi_G)_*\bigl(\kappa\,\omega_Z\,\pi_X^*u\bigr),
$$
where pullback, multiplication by a density, proper pushforward, and $C_Z$ use the conventions of the preceding definition. In local fiber coordinates this is integration of $u$ over the incidence fibers with weight $\kappa$ and density $\omega_Z$. The hypotheses on proper support ensure this transform is defined for every compactly supported input. This is the class treated on this page; no noisy-data or stability assertion is included.

For an analytic double fibration with incidence cotangent relation $C_Z\subset(T^*G\setminus0)\times(T^*X\setminus0)$, let
$$
\pi_L:C_Z\longrightarrow T^*G\setminus0,\qquad \pi_L(g,\eta;x,\xi)=(g,\eta).
$$
The double fibration satisfies the global Bolker condition if $\pi_L$ is an injective immersion. The Bolker condition holds at a specified point $c=(g,\eta;x,\xi)\in C_Z$ if the full fiber over its data covector is the singleton $\pi_L^{-1}(g,\eta)=\{c\}$ and $d\pi_L|_c$ is injective. Thus the pointwise condition has both a fiber-uniqueness clause, which excludes every other relation point over the same data covector even outside a chosen chart, and a local differential-rank clause.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded incidence submanifold of codimension $k>0$, and let $(g_0,x_0)\in Z$. Choose coordinates near this point and a submersion $F:G\times X\to\mathbb R^k$ with $Z=\{F=0\}$. Write $F=(F_1,\ldots,F_k)$. For every $\tau\in\mathbb R^k\setminus\{0\}$, the conormal covector at $(g,x)\in Z$ is
$$
(g,x;D_gF(g,x)^T\tau,\ D_xF(g,x)^T\tau).
$$
Consequently the incidence kernel has local delta representation $b(g,x)\delta(F(g,x))|dg\,dx|$, with a smooth density coefficient $b$, and its cotangent relation consists exactly of
$$
(g,D_gF^T\tau;\ x,-D_xF^T\tau),\qquad (g,x)\in Z,\quad \tau\ne0.
$$
No general Fourier-integral-operator composition calculus is used.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

For $R>0$, the sphere $S_R^{m-1}=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:\|x\|_2=R\}$ is the regular level $F^{-1}(R^2)$ of $F(x)=\|x\|_2^2$. At $x\in S_R^{m-1}$,
$$T_xS_R^{m-1}=x^\perp=\{h:\langle x,h\rangle=0\}.$$

Let $f$ be a real analytic map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, $f$ has a real analytic local inverse near $f(a)$. Let $P(x,y)$ be real analytic near $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^k$, $k\ge1$, with $P(a,b)=0$ and $D_yP(a,b)$ invertible. On sufficiently small neighborhoods its zero set is exactly the graph of a unique real analytic $y=g(x)$ with $g(a)=b$.

Let $a<b$, let $\varepsilon>0$, and let
$$F:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\times[a,b]\longrightarrow M$$
be a smooth map, smooth up to the two time endpoints. It is a **geodesic
variation** when for every $s\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ the longitudinal
curve $t\mapsto F(s,t)$ is an affinely parametrized geodesic; equivalently,
$$D_t\partial_tF(s,t)=0.$$
The central geodesic is $\gamma(t)=F(0,t)$, and its **variation field** is
$$V(t)=\left.\partial_sF(s,t)\right|_{s=0}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M.$$
This is the variation-field construction in
[[def-smooth-variation-and-variation-field-of-a-curve]], with the additional
condition that every longitudinal curve is geodesic. No fixed-endpoint
condition is imposed: $V(a)$ and $V(b)$ may be nonzero. Constant geodesics are
allowed, including on zero-dimensional manifolds; dimension one is covered by
the same definition. If $M$ is empty, there is no such map on the nonempty
parameter interval, so the definition assigns no variation object.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, let $I$ be a nondegenerate interval,
and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an affinely parametrized geodesic. For a smooth
vector field $J$ along $\gamma$, write $D_tJ$ for its covariant derivative
along $\gamma$ and $D_t^2J=D_t(D_tJ)$, using
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]. The curvature operator $R$ has the
convention
$$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z,$$
as fixed by [[lem-covariant-derivatives-commute-up-to-curvature-in-a-two-parameter-variation]]
and used in [[def-riemann-curvature-four-tensor]]. A smooth field $J$ is a
**Jacobi field** along $\gamma$ when it satisfies the Jacobi equation
$$D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$$
throughout $I$. We write $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ for the set of these fields.

The interval is required to have nonempty interior so that the covariant
derivatives are defined; if an endpoint is included, the equation there uses
the one-sided derivatives of the smooth field. Constant geodesics are included:
when $\dot\gamma=0$, the curvature term vanishes and the equation is
$D_t^2J=0$. On a zero-dimensional manifold the only field is zero, so the
equation holds. In dimension one the same equation and curvature convention
apply without a separate restriction. The definition classifies a specified
field and geodesic and makes no existence choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary of dimension $n\ge0$,
let $a<b$, and let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be an affinely parametrized geodesic.
Define
$$\mathcal K_\gamma(a,b):=\{J\in\mathcal J(\gamma):J(a)=0,\ J(b)=0\}.$$
This is a finite-dimensional real vector space. The points $\gamma(a)$ and
$\gamma(b)$ are **conjugate along $\gamma$** exactly when
$\mathcal K_\gamma(a,b)$ contains a nonzero Jacobi field. For a conjugate pair,
its **multiplicity** is $\dim_\mathbb R\mathcal K_\gamma(a,b)$. If $\gamma$ is
constant, then $\mathcal K_\gamma(a,b)=\{0\}$ and the endpoints are not
conjugate. If $\gamma$ is nonconstant, then
$\dim_\mathbb R\mathcal K_\gamma(a,b)\le n-1$. Included endpoint derivatives
are one-sided. No completeness or choice axiom is assumed.

Let $n\geq1$, and give
$$S^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:\langle x,x\rangle=1\}$$
the round metric induced by the Euclidean inner product. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior. For any supplied $t_0\in I$, a nonconstant affinely parametrized geodesic $\gamma:I\to S^n$ has constant speed $c>0$ and can be written
$$\gamma(t)=\cos(c(t-t_0))p+\sin(c(t-t_0))u,$$
where $p=\gamma(t_0)$ and $u=\gamma'(t_0)/c$ are orthonormal. Its image is therefore an arc of the great circle $S^n\cap\operatorname{span}\{p,u\}$; the corresponding maximal geodesic has the whole great circle as its image. Conversely, every such constant-speed parametrization of a great circle is a geodesic. Constant geodesics are obtained separately by taking $\gamma(t)=p$.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, let $a<b$, let $\varepsilon>0$, and
let
$$F:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\times[a,b]\longrightarrow M$$
be a smooth geodesic variation, so every longitudinal curve
$t\mapsto F(s,t)$ is an affinely parametrized geodesic. Set
$$\gamma(t)=F(0,t),\qquad V(t)=\left.\partial_sF(s,t)\right|_{s=0}.$$
Then $V$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$:
$$D_t^2V+R(V,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$$
on $[a,b]$, using one-sided derivatives at included endpoints. No fixed
endpoint condition is imposed; constant geodesics and dimension zero are
included. This implication uses no axiom of choice.

derivations.claim: Put $F(n,x)=n\cdot x$ on $S^2\times S^2$. At a point with $F=0$, the vector $x$ lies in $T_nS^2$ by [F5], and the tangent variation $(\dot n,\dot x)=(x,0)$ satisfies $dF(\dot n,\dot x)=x\cdot x=1$. Thus $dF\ne0$; [F6] makes $Z=F^{-1}(0)$ an analytic hypersurface of dimension $3$ in the $4$-dimensional product.

A tangent vector to $Z$ satisfies $x\cdot\dot n+n\cdot\dot x=0$. Given any $\dot n\in T_nS^2$, set $\dot x=-(x\cdot\dot n)n$; then $\dot x\in T_xS^2$ by [F5], and the tangent equation holds. Hence $\pi_G$ is a submersion. Given any $\dot x\in T_xS^2$, set $\dot n=-(n\cdot\dot x)x$; the same calculation proves $\pi_X$ is a submersion. Both maps are analytic restrictions of product projections. Since $Z$ is compact, $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. The density induced by the positive-definite analytic product round metric has strictly positive analytic coefficient in every local incidence chart. The dimensions satisfy $4>3>2\ge2$, so [F1] applies.

The defining differential on tangent vectors to the product is $dF=(x^\flat,n^\flat)$ by the metric identification [F4]. Therefore by [F3] the relation at $(n,x)$ consists of $ (n,\eta;x,\xi)=(n,\tau x^\flat;x,-\tau n^\flat),\qquad \tau\ne0. $ At the antipodal point $-x$, choose multiplier $-\tau$. Its data covector is $(-\tau)(-x)^\flat=\tau x^\flat$, the same as at $x$, while the object point changes from $x$ to $-x$. Both are nonzero relation points. Hence the left projection is not injective, and [F2] implies failure of global Bolker.

Let $v=n\times x$, a unit tangent vector at $x$. For $s$ near zero put $n_s=\cos(s)n+\sin(s)v$, $v_s=n_s\times x$, and $ \gamma_s(t)=\cos(t)x+\sin(t)v_s,\qquad 0\le t\le\pi. $ Each $n_s$ is a unit vector orthogonal to $x$, and $v_s$ is a unit vector orthogonal to $x$; hence $\gamma_s$ parametrizes a great circle at unit speed and is a geodesic by [F10]. Thus [F7] makes this a geodesic variation. Its endpoints are fixed: $\gamma_s(0)=x$ and $\gamma_s(\pi)=-x$. Differentiating in $s$ at zero gives $ J(t)=\left.\partial_s\gamma_s(t)\right|_{s=0} =\sin(t)(v\times x)=-\sin(t)n, $ because $(n\times x)\times x=-n$ when $n\cdot x=0$ and $|x|=1$. By [F11] this field is Jacobi and hence satisfies the Jacobi equation in [F8]. It is nonzero for $0<t<\pi$ and vanishes at both endpoints, so [F9] makes the endpoints conjugate. The proof uses no choice axiom; the sphere has no boundary, so this example lies outside the simple-surface hypotheses.

Let $f$ be holomorphic on $D(a,R)$ and let $0<r<R$. Suppose $M\ge0$ and

$$|f(\zeta)|\le M\qquad\text{whenever }|\zeta-a|=r.$$

Then, for every $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$|f^{(n)}(a)|\le\frac{n!M}{r^n}.$$

Let $\phi$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood of $0\in\mathbb C^n$, with $d\phi(0)=0$ and complex Hessian $H=\phi''(0)$ invertible. There is a local biholomorphic coordinate map $w=\Psi(z)$ with $\Psi(0)=0$ such that
$$
\phi(z)=\phi(0)+\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^n w_j^2.
$$
Its linear part satisfies $(\det D\Psi(0))^2=\det H$. For a continuous parameter family of invertible Hessians $H(p)$, near any fixed parameter $p_0$ the determinant remains in a disc avoiding $0$; choosing one square root at $p_0$ therefore fixes a continuous branch on that neighborhood. If $\operatorname{Re}H$ is positive definite, then
$$
\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\lambda x^THx/2}\,dx =(2\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}(\det H)^{-1/2},\qquad \lambda>0,
$$
with the integral interpreted as an absolutely convergent improper integral and the branch analytically continued from real positive-definite matrices. Finally, deforming a holomorphic contour preserves the integral of a holomorphic top-degree form when the contours are homologous through a region of holomorphy and the swept boundary integrals tend to zero.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded open set, let $\Phi$ be holomorphic on a complex neighborhood of $\overline U$, and let $a\in C_c^\infty(U)$ have a holomorphic extension near $0$. Assume $0\in\operatorname{supp}a$, $\Phi(0)=\Phi_0$, $d\Phi(0)=0$, and $d\Phi(x)\ne0$ at every $x\in\operatorname{supp}a\setminus\{0\}$. Let $H=-i\Phi''(0)$ be complex symmetric with positive-definite real part. Assume there are $r,c_0,d_0>0$ such that
$$
\operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge c_0|x|^2 \quad(|x|\le r),\qquad \operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge d_0 \quad(x\in\operatorname{supp}a,\ |x|\ge r).
$$
Let $\chi_N$ be the finite-order cutoff sequence equal to one on a fixed neighborhood of $0$, with $0\le\chi_N\le1$, and supported where these phase hypotheses hold. For every integer $N\ge1$ and every $\lambda\ge1$, put $I_N(\lambda)=\int e^{i\lambda\Phi(x)}a(x)\chi_N(x)\,dx$. There are coefficients $c_j$ determined by the full Taylor series of the phase and amplitude at $0$ and constants $C,\delta>0$, independent of $N,\lambda$, such that
$$
I_N(\lambda)=e^{i\lambda\Phi_0}(2\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}(\det H)^{-1/2} \left(\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\lambda^{-j}\right)+E_N(\lambda),
$$
$$
|c_j|\le C^{j+1}j!,\qquad |e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)|\le C^{N+1}N!\lambda^{-N-n/2}+Ce^{-\delta\lambda}.
$$
The square-root branch is fixed by the preceding holomorphic Morse/Gaussian-contour lemma, and $c_0=a(0)$. Taking $N=\lfloor\epsilon\lambda\rfloor$ for sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$ and sufficiently large $\lambda$ makes the normalized remainder $e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)=O(e^{-\delta_2\lambda})$ for some $\delta_2>0$. The expansion includes every coefficient through the stated truncation order; it is not only a leading-term estimate.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $K\subset U$ be compact. There are constants $A,C>0$ and functions $\chi_N\in C_c^\infty(U)$ for each integer $N\ge1$ such that $0\le\chi_N\le1$, $\chi_N=1$ on a fixed neighborhood of $K$, and
$$
|\partial^\alpha\chi_N(x)|\le C(AN)^{|\alpha|} \qquad (x\in\mathbb R^n,\ |\alpha|\le N).
$$
These are smooth compact cutoffs; no compactly supported analytic function is asserted.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb C^m$ be
holomorphic, and let $a\in U$. If $\det J_{\mathbb C}F(a)\ne0$, then there are
open neighbourhoods $U_0\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $V_0$ of $F(a)$ such that
$F|_{U_0}:U_0\to V_0$ is biholomorphic.

If $G:V_0\to U_0$ denotes the inverse, then

$$DG(w)=DF(G(w))^{-1}\qquad(w\in V_0).$$

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

For a formal holomorphic symbol $p=\sum_{j\ge0}h^jp_j(x,\xi)$, with $|p_j|\le C^{j+1}j!$ on a fixed polydisc, define $ p\#q=\sum_{j,k,\gamma}\frac{h^{j+k+|\gamma|}}{i^{|\gamma|}\gamma!} (\partial_\xi^\gamma p_j)(\partial_x^\gamma q_k). $ There are finitely many terms in each degree. Associativity follows directly by applying the product rule to the two triple products: splitting a multi-index $\gamma=\mu+\nu$ contributes $\gamma!/(\mu!\nu!)$, which cancels its denominator and leaves identical terms. The map $p\mapsto P=p(x,\xi+hD_x)$, with $D_x=\partial_x/i$, respects this product; expansion by the product rule gives the displayed formula.

The actual contour realization is [F8], with $\rho=-\operatorname{Im}S$ and $h=\lambda^{-1}$. In fixed-offset coordinates $y=x+w$, its oriented volume and prefactor give the explicit formula
$$
A_hv(x)=\left(\frac{R}{\pi h}\right)^n\int_{|w|\le r}\exp\left(\frac{-iw\cdot S_x(x)-R|w|^2}{h}\right)p\bigl(x,x+w,S_x(x)-iR\overline w;h\bigr)v(x+w;h)\,dL(w).
$$
Here $dL$ is Euclidean $2n$-dimensional measure, the phase-space cycle and its orientation are exactly those of [F8], and $R,r$ are fixed within the common holomorphy neighborhood. The Gaussian bound and amplitude-$1$ identity are the specified operator theorem [F8]; equivalently, for amplitude $1$ the holomorphic factor $e^{-iw\cdot S_x(x)/h}v(x+w;h)$ has constant Taylor coefficient $v(x;h)$ and all positive-degree holomorphic monomials have zero angular integral. The remaining Gaussian tail is exponentially small in the weighted germ. For this pluriharmonic weight the fixed-offset formula is holomorphic in $x$; it also specifies precisely the previously implicit cycle and measure. The fixed-derivative real-localization bounds used later are [F10], rather than an assertion obtained solely from this formal identity.

Here are estimates for this formal algebra that also control its inverse. Use nested complex $x$ neighborhoods $\Omega_t$, $0<t<t_0<1$, whose boundary separation is at least $t-s$, and keep $\xi$ in a smaller fixed polydisc. Write $P=\sum h^kP_k$, where $P_k$ has differential order at most $k$. Cauchy's inequality, first in the fixed $\xi$ polydisc and then in $x$, gives $ \|P_k\|_{t,s}\le C^{k+1} k^k(t-s)^{-k},\qquad 0<s<t<t_0. $ Indeed a term with $j+|\gamma|=k$ costs at most $C^{k+1}j!\gamma!(t-s)^{-|\gamma|}$; $j!\gamma!\le k!\le k^k$, $t-s<1$, and the number of terms is at most exponential in $k$. For $k=0$ use $0^0=1$. Let $f_k(P)$ be the least admissible constant in $\|P_k\|_{t,s}\le f_k(P)k^k(t-s)^{-k}$. If $R=PQ$, choose the intermediate radius with $r-s=j(t-s)/(j+k)$ for the term $P_jQ_k$. Then $ f_\ell(PQ)\le\sum_{j+k=\ell}f_j(P)f_k(Q). $ The endpoint cases use the same estimate without an intermediate loss. Consequently $\|P\|_\rho=\sum\rho^kf_k(P)$ is submultiplicative whenever finite. Conversely $p_k=P_k1$, evaluated with a fixed radius loss, satisfies $|p_k|\le C^{k+1}k^k\le (eC)^{k+1}k!$; the last inequality follows by integrating $\log t$ from $1$ to $k$. These estimates are on one fixed smaller neighborhood, independent of $k$.

If $p_0\ne0$, shrink so $1/p_0$ is bounded holomorphic. The formal product $p\#(1/p_0)=1-r$ has $r_0=0$ and finite $\|r\|_\rho$ for small $\rho$ by step 2.1; decreasing $\rho$ makes this norm less than $1/2$. Thus $ q=(1/p_0)\#\sum_{\ell\ge0}r^{\#\ell} $ has finite norm, because in each degree its defining sum is finite and the geometric norm sum is at most $2$. It follows that $q_j$ have factorial bounds on a fixed smaller neighborhood. This gives a right inverse. The identical construction on the other side gives a left inverse; associativity shows they agree. Truncating at $j<\epsilon/h$ realizes these symbols. A term with index $j$ has modulus at most $C(Chj)^j$; for $j\le\epsilon/h$ and $C\epsilon<1/2$ it is at most $C2^{-j}$. Two admissible truncations therefore differ by $O(e^{-c/h})$, also in every fixed derivative by [F1].

The actual composition and inverse statements invoked here are the external results [F9]–[F10]. The following calculation identifies their specialization and symbol; it is not an independent reconstruction of that analytic contour calculus. Products of these kernels are actual iterated contour integrals. All weights needed here are of this form, with $S$ the packet phase and its holomorphic critical value; thus the saddle phases used for contour comparison are holomorphic. Their composed contour is good: if the inner integration has loss $c|y-y(z)|^2$ and the outer one loss $c|z-z(x)|^2$, their sum controls the square distance from the combined critical point, since the critical-point maps have bounded derivatives. The holomorphic Morse coordinates [F2] identify this contour and the contour obtained by doing the integrations in the other order with graphs over a common negative-definite real subspace. Such graphs have slope less than one after a linear scaling; their straight interpolation has the same positive quadratic margin on a smaller ball. Stokes therefore changes the order and reduces the composition, with exponentially small boundary errors. Taylor expansion in $y-x$, followed by integration by parts in $\theta$, gives the full symbol $ p_{\mathrm{red}}(x,\xi;h)\sim\sum_\gamma\frac{h^{|\gamma|}}{i^{|\gamma|}\gamma!} \partial_\xi^\gamma\partial_y^\gamma p(x,y,\xi;h)|_{y=x}. $ For a product this is exactly the $\#$ formula in step 1.1. To estimate rather than just manipulate this expansion, apply [F3] on the good contour after its quadratic normalization. Cauchy bounds for the analytic amplitudes give $C^{N+1}N!h^N$ for the remainder after total degree $N$; each of the finitely many symbol indices contributes the convolution estimates in step 2.1. Taking $N=\lfloor\epsilon/h\rfloor$ makes this $O(e^{-c/h})$. The actual operator consequences are supplied by [F9]–[F10]: a zero reduced symbol acts by an exponentially small operator, and the inverse symbol of step 3.1 gives an actual two-sided inverse modulo such errors. $$
G\xleftarrow{\ \pi_G\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi_X\ }X

$$
\dim G+\dim X>\dim Z>\dim G\ge\dim X.
$$

Let $\omega_Z$ be a nowhere vanishing real-analytic smooth density on $Z$ and let $\kappa\colon Z\to\mathbb C$ be real analytic and nowhere zero. For a compactly supported distribution $u$ on $X$, the weighted transform is the distributional density
$$
Ru=(\pi_G)_*\bigl(\kappa\,\omega_Z\,\pi_X^*u\bigr),
$$
where pullback, multiplication by a density, proper pushforward, and $C_Z$ use the conventions of the preceding definition. In local fiber coordinates this is integration of $u$ over the incidence fibers with weight $\kappa$ and density $\omega_Z$. The hypotheses on proper support ensure this transform is defined for every compactly supported input. This is the class treated on this page; no noisy-data or stability assertion is included.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.

In these coordinates the transpose data packet has integrals of the form $ \int e^{i\lambda\Psi(t,x;q,\omega)}b(t,x)\chi(z(t,x))\,dt,\qquad \Psi=(q-z(t,x))\cdot\omega+\frac i2|q-z(t,x)|^2, $ where $b$ is analytic and $\chi$ is a data cutoff. At incidence points $z(t,x)=q$, $\partial_t\Psi=-D_tz^T\omega$. If this vanished in every fiber direction, then $\omega$ would annihilate the vertical tangent of $\pi_X$ and extend to a nonzero conormal $(\omega,-\xi)$ of $Z$; the submersion hypotheses ensure both components are nonzero. This would be a relation point over $(q,\omega,x)$, excluded by the neighborhoods just chosen.

On the compact incidence portion over $\overline V$ and $K_1$, the no-relation property from step 1.1 gives a positive lower bound for $\max_j|\partial_{t_j}\Psi|$ when $z=q$ and $(q,\omega)$ ranges over smaller compactly contained neighborhoods of $(z_0,\omega_0)$. By continuity, shrink the data chart, direction neighborhood and fiber charts so this lower bound persists whenever $|z-q|$ is sufficiently small. A finite refinement therefore gives the uniform alternative on each piece, for $x$ in a neighborhood of $K$ and $(q,\omega)$ near the supplied data point: either $|z-q|\ge d>0$, or one fiber coordinate satisfies $|\partial_{t_j}\Psi|\ge d>0$. The first pieces have Gaussian exponential decay in every fixed object derivative. For the second pieces shrink the analytic neighborhoods so $1/\partial_{t_j}\Psi$ is holomorphic and has uniform factorial derivative bounds by [F4]. The data cutoff can be chosen equal to one on the central data neighborhood. Its transition contributes only pieces of the first type, so it is never differentiated to an order growing with $\lambda$ in the second estimate.

For integration by parts choose finite-order localizers in the finitely many refined fiber charts. They can form an exact partition near the incidence compact without reciprocal derivatives: if $\chi_{j,N}$ are the cutoffs in [F3], take $\rho_{j,N}=\chi_{j,N}\prod_{\ell<j}(1-\chi_{\ell,N})$. At every point of the compact at least one $\chi_{j,N}$ is identically one on a fixed neighborhood. Hence $\sum_j\rho_{j,N}=1$ there. There are a fixed finite number of factors; the product rule gives $|\partial^\alpha\rho_{j,N}|\le C(CN)^{|\alpha|}$ for $|\alpha|\le N$. Extend the construction to a fixed slightly larger compact in the incidence charts, so all object derivatives through any fixed order $m$ preserve the exact partition identity near $K$. Use the sequence indexed by $N+m$.

On a nonstationary piece use $L=(i\lambda\partial_{t_j}\Psi)^{-1}\partial_{t_j}$, so $Le^{i\lambda\Psi}=e^{i\lambda\Psi}$. There are no boundary terms because the localizers have compact support in the chart. After $N$ integrations by parts the integrand is $e^{i\lambda\Psi}(L^*)^N(b\rho_{j,N+m})$. The factorial coefficient bounds and the product rule give $ \|(L^*)^N(b\rho_{j,N+m})\|_\infty \le C^{N+1}\lambda^{-N}\sum_{k=0}^N\frac{N!}{k!}(C(N+m))^k \le C_m(C_m N/\lambda)^N $ for $N\ge m+1$. To obtain the first bound, expand each adjoint as a first-order derivative plus its differentiated analytic coefficient; induction distributes $k$ derivatives to the localizer and bounds the remaining analytic derivatives by $C^{N+1}N!/k!$. In the second bound use $N!\le N^N$ and $\sum_{k\le N}(C(N+m))^k/k!\le e^{C(N+m)}$. The bounded integration volumes and $|e^{i\lambda\Psi}|\le1$ leave the same bound for the integral. Applying $m$ object derivatives first adds at most a fixed power of $\lambda$ and $N$; the same induction with $N+m$ gives $C_m\lambda^{M_m}N^{M_m}(C_mN/\lambda)^N$. Fix this $m$ and take $N=\lfloor\epsilon_m\lambda\rfloor$ with $C_m\epsilon_m<1/2$. The result is $O(e^{-c_m\lambda})$.

The transpose packet coefficient is independent of $N$ because the partition is exact near the support. Summing the finitely many estimates in steps 2.1 and 4.1 proves the asserted $C^m$ estimate on a fixed neighborhood of $K$. Take $m$ to be the finite distributional order in [F2] and pair with $u$. It follows that the data Gaussian FBI pairing of $Ru$ is uniformly exponentially small. The definition of analytic wavefront gives the conclusion. This proof uses neither an unproved wavefront pushforward theorem nor a compact analytic bump.
