Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. A distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on compactly supported smooth densities on $M$. Its topology is generated locally by the fixed-support seminorms $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha\varphi|$, followed by the locally convex test-function topology. In a chart $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ a test density is $\varphi(x)|dx|$; under a coordinate change it transforms by the absolute Jacobian. A distribution is compactly supported when its support, the complement of its largest vanishing open set, is compact.

For a smooth submersion $p:Y\to M$, define the pullback $p^*u$ by transposing fiber integration: in submersion coordinates $p(x,v)=x$,
$$
\langle p^*u,\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|\rangle =\left\langle u,\left(\int\psi(x,v)|dv|\right)|dx|\right\rangle.
$$
The absolute density quotient gives the fiber density in other submersion coordinates. For a distributional density $V$ on $Y$, meaning a continuous functional on compactly supported smooth scalar functions, define its support by the same largest-vanishing-open-set rule. If $q:Y\to M$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$, then for a test function $\varphi$ on $M$ the set $q^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\varphi)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose a smooth compact cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near this set and define the pushforward by
$$
\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta(\varphi\circ q)\rangle.
$$
The support property makes this independent of $\beta$; the cutoff is needed because $\varphi\circ q$ need not be compactly supported on all of $Y$.
A smooth density $\mu$ times a distribution $u$ in the test-density convention is the distributional density $\mu u$ defined by $\langle\mu u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\varphi\mu\rangle$.

Let $Z\subseteq G\times X$ be an embedded submanifold whose two projections are submersions. For a smooth density $\omega_Z$ on $Z$, its incidence delta kernel is the distributional density
$$
\langle K_Z,\Phi\rangle=\int_Z\Phi|_Z\,\omega_Z.
$$
In coordinates $(g,x)=(u,t)$ with $Z=\{t=0\}$, this is the delta distribution in the $t$ variables paired with the chosen density on $Z$. The conormal bundle and associated cotangent relation are
$$
N^*Z=\{(z,\zeta)\in T^*(G\times X):z\in Z,\ \zeta|_{T_zZ}=0\}, \qquad C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}.
$$
Here $N^*Z\setminus0$ removes the zero covector, and the minus sign is the distribution-kernel convention for an operator from $X$ to $G$. Since both projections are submersions, every nonzero conormal in this relation has both $\eta\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$. An analytic incidence kernel means that $Z$, its local defining maps, and the coefficients of $\omega_Z$ are real analytic. This definition covers the incidence kernels used below; it does not assert a general Fourier-integral-operator calculus.

An analytic double fibration is a diagram of real-analytic manifolds and real-analytic submersions
$$
G\xleftarrow{\ \pi_G\ }Z\xrightarrow{\ \pi_X\ }X
$$
such that $Z$ is embedded in $G\times X$, both projections are submersions, and
$$
\dim G+\dim X>\dim Z>\dim G\ge\dim X.
$$
Write $C_Z=\{(g,\eta;x,\xi):(g,x;\eta,-\xi)\in N^*Z\setminus0\}$ for the incidence cotangent relation. Assume $\pi_G$ is proper on $\pi_X^{-1}(K)$ for every compact $K\subset X$. Let $\omega_Z$ be a nowhere vanishing real-analytic smooth density on $Z$ and let $\kappa\colon Z\to\mathbb C$ be real analytic and nowhere zero. For a compactly supported distribution $u$ on $X$, the weighted transform is the distributional density
$$
Ru=(\pi_G)_*\bigl(\kappa\,\omega_Z\,\pi_X^*u\bigr),
$$
where pullback, multiplication by a density, proper pushforward, and $C_Z$ use the conventions of the preceding definition. In local fiber coordinates this is integration of $u$ over the incidence fibers with weight $\kappa$ and density $\omega_Z$. The hypotheses on proper support ensure this transform is defined for every compactly supported input. This is the class treated on this page; no noisy-data or stability assertion is included.

Let $f$ be a real analytic map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, $f$ has a real analytic local inverse near $f(a)$. Let $P(x,y)$ be real analytic near $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^k$, $k\ge1$, with $P(a,b)=0$ and $D_yP(a,b)$ invertible. On sufficiently small neighborhoods its zero set is exactly the graph of a unique real analytic $y=g(x)$ with $g(a)=b$.

Let $\phi$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood of $0\in\mathbb C^n$, with $d\phi(0)=0$ and complex Hessian $H=\phi''(0)$ invertible. There is a local biholomorphic coordinate map $w=\Psi(z)$ with $\Psi(0)=0$ such that
$$
\phi(z)=\phi(0)+\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^n w_j^2.
$$
Its linear part satisfies $(\det D\Psi(0))^2=\det H$. For a continuous parameter family of invertible Hessians $H(p)$, near any fixed parameter $p_0$ the determinant remains in a disc avoiding $0$; choosing one square root at $p_0$ therefore fixes a continuous branch on that neighborhood. If $\operatorname{Re}H$ is positive definite, then
$$
\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\lambda x^THx/2}\,dx =(2\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}(\det H)^{-1/2},\qquad \lambda>0,
$$
with the integral interpreted as an absolutely convergent improper integral and the branch analytically continued from real positive-definite matrices. Finally, deforming a holomorphic contour preserves the integral of a holomorphic top-degree form when the contours are homologous through a region of holomorphy and the swept boundary integrals tend to zero.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded open set, let $\Phi$ be holomorphic on a complex neighborhood of $\overline U$, and let $a\in C_c^\infty(U)$ have a holomorphic extension near $0$. Assume $0\in\operatorname{supp}a$, $\Phi(0)=\Phi_0$, $d\Phi(0)=0$, and $d\Phi(x)\ne0$ at every $x\in\operatorname{supp}a\setminus\{0\}$. Let $H=-i\Phi''(0)$ be complex symmetric with positive-definite real part. Assume there are $r,c_0,d_0>0$ such that
$$
\operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge c_0|x|^2 \quad(|x|\le r),\qquad \operatorname{Im}(\Phi(x)-\Phi_0)\ge d_0 \quad(x\in\operatorname{supp}a,\ |x|\ge r).
$$
Let $\chi_N$ be the finite-order cutoff sequence equal to one on a fixed neighborhood of $0$, with $0\le\chi_N\le1$, and supported where these phase hypotheses hold. For every integer $N\ge1$ and every $\lambda\ge1$, put $I_N(\lambda)=\int e^{i\lambda\Phi(x)}a(x)\chi_N(x)\,dx$. There are coefficients $c_j$ determined by the full Taylor series of the phase and amplitude at $0$ and constants $C,\delta>0$, independent of $N,\lambda$, such that
$$
I_N(\lambda)=e^{i\lambda\Phi_0}(2\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}(\det H)^{-1/2} \left(\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}c_j\lambda^{-j}\right)+E_N(\lambda),
$$
$$
|c_j|\le C^{j+1}j!,\qquad |e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)|\le C^{N+1}N!\lambda^{-N-n/2}+Ce^{-\delta\lambda}.
$$
The square-root branch is fixed by the preceding holomorphic Morse/Gaussian-contour lemma, and $c_0=a(0)$. Taking $N=\lfloor\epsilon\lambda\rfloor$ for sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$ and sufficiently large $\lambda$ makes the normalized remainder $e^{-i\lambda\Phi_0}E_N(\lambda)=O(e^{-\delta_2\lambda})$ for some $\delta_2>0$. The expansion includes every coefficient through the stated truncation order; it is not only a leading-term estimate.

Work near $(q_0,p_0)\in\mathbb R^n\times(\mathbb R^n\setminus0)$. A normalized positive analytic packet phase is a holomorphic function $\phi(y,q,p)$ on a fixed complex neighborhood of the indicated real variables, such that, for real arguments,
$$
\phi(q,q,p)=0,\qquad \partial_y\phi(q,q,p)=-p,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\phi(y,q,p)\ge c|y-q|^2
$$
for some $c>0$. A classical analytic amplitude is realized on each smaller complex neighborhood by
$$
a(y,q,p;\lambda)=\sum_{j<\epsilon\lambda}a_j(y,q,p)\lambda^{-j},\qquad \sup|a_j|\le C^{j+1}j!,
$$
with sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$. Changing $\epsilon$ to a smaller positive number changes the realization by an exponentially small function on a smaller neighborhood. An elliptic amplitude has $a_0(q_0,q_0,p_0)\ne0$.

For a distribution $u$ localized to a sufficiently small fixed compact neighborhood of $q_0$, the uniform exponential decay of
$$
\langle u(y),a(y,q,p;\lambda)e^{i\lambda\phi(y,q,p)}\rangle
$$
for $(q,p)$ in a neighborhood of $(q_0,p_0)$ is independent of the normalized positive phase and elliptic classical analytic amplitude. Smooth fixed cutoffs equal to one near the packet centers are understood. This criterion agrees with the Gaussian criterion with unit directions and arbitrary $\lambda\ge1$.

More precisely, after shrinking the parameter neighborhood $W$, every other such packet $v_\beta$ with $\beta$ in a smaller $W_0\Subset W$ has a representation
$$
v_\beta(y;\lambda)=\int_W a(y,\alpha;\lambda)e^{i\lambda\phi(y,\alpha)}K(\beta,\alpha;\lambda)\,d\alpha+R_\beta(y;\lambda),
$$
where $|K|\le C\lambda^L$ and $\|R_\beta\|_{C^m}\le C_m e^{-c_m\lambda}$ on the fixed localization compact, for every fixed $m$. There is a representation in the reverse direction as well. All estimates are uniform on the stated smaller neighborhoods. Thus the inverse is an actual local operator modulo exponentially small errors, rather than just a formal inverse series.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb C^m$ be
holomorphic, and let $a\in U$. If $\det J_{\mathbb C}F(a)\ne0$, then there are
open neighbourhoods $U_0\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $V_0$ of $F(a)$ such that
$F|_{U_0}:U_0\to V_0$ is biholomorphic.

If $G:V_0\to U_0$ denotes the inverse, then

$$DG(w)=DF(G(w))^{-1}\qquad(w\in V_0).$$

derivations.claim: Choose analytic fiber coordinates for $\pi_X$, $ (t,x)\longmapsto (z(t,x),x)\in Z,\qquad t\in\mathbb R^d. $ The matrix $D_tz$ is injective because this map is an immersion with $x$ retained. The conormal equations from [F1] are $ (D_tz)^Tp=0,\qquad \xi=(D_xz)^Tp. $ The first equations define an analytic bundle of rank $\dim G-d$ in the $p$ variables, so $(t,x,p)$ with these equations parameterize $C_Z$ locally. The map to data cotangent space is $(t,x,p)\mapsto(z(t,x),p)$. Its derivative is injective by the hypothesis; selecting a full-rank coordinate minor and applying [F3] makes it an analytic embedding on a smaller neighborhood. Denote its image by $V$.

We make the exact packet resolution explicit, without importing a Fourier inversion theorem with an additional choice assumption. In $\mathbb R^n$, set $ m^\lambda_{a,b}(y)=2^{-n/2}\pi^{-3n/4}\lambda^{3n/4}e^{i\lambda y\cdot b-\lambda|y-a|^2/2}. $ Then, with the frequency integral interpreted by the indicated Gaussian regularization, $ u(y)=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int e^{-\varepsilon|b|^2}\langle u,\overline{m^\lambda_{a,b}}\rangle m^\lambda_{a,b}(y)\,da\,db $ in distributions. Indeed the $b$ integral is $(\pi/\varepsilon)^{n/2}e^{-\lambda^2|y-y'|^2/(4\varepsilon)}$, by completing the square and the Gaussian contour formula [F4]. The $a$ integral is $(\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}e^{-\lambda|y-y'|^2/4}$. Including the squared normalization, their product is a Gaussian kernel in $y-y'$ with mass tending to $1$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and width tending to $0$. Pairing against a compact test, each fixed derivative converges uniformly on the support of $u$: split into a small translation neighborhood controlled by uniform continuity and its Gaussian tail. Thus [F1] justifies the distributional limit. The limiting normalization is exactly one, as also follows by multiplying $(2\pi/\lambda)^n$ and $(\pi/\lambda)^{n/2}$ by the squared packet constant. Applying this identity on data space, or directly transposing the incidence integral, gives the same object kernel as direct transposition of the incidence integral.

The paired map $\chi:V\to T^*X$ is a submersion. Here is a local linear-algebra proof. On $C_Z$, the one-form $p\,dz-\xi\,dx$ vanishes by the conormal equations; hence its differential also vanishes. The tangent space $L$ of $C_Z$ therefore is isotropic for the nondegenerate bilinear alternating form $dp\wedge dz-d\xi\wedge dx$. Its dimension is $\dim G+\dim X$, half the ambient dimension, so $L$ equals its alternating orthogonal complement. If $d\pi_R(L)$ were a proper subspace, the nondegenerate form $d\xi\wedge dx$ would give a nonzero vector $w$ orthogonal to it. Then $(0,w)$ would be orthogonal to $L$, hence in $L$, and would lie in the kernel of $d\pi_L$. This contradicts injectivity. Thus $d\pi_R$ is onto. The argument uses only the matrix criterion for an alternating form to be nondegenerate and the dimension formula for its orthogonal complement. By [F3], $\chi$ has a local analytic section $v=v(Q,P)$ onto an open neighborhood of $(x_0,\xi_0)$.

Pair $Ru$ with the data Gaussian and use the typed transpose in [F1]. Up to the harmless unit factor $e^{i\lambda q\cdot p}$ its object kernel is $ K_\lambda(x,v)=\int e^{i\lambda\Psi(t,x,v)}b(t,x)\,dt,\qquad \Psi=-z(t,x)\cdot p+\frac i2|z(t,x)-q|^2. $ The analytic coefficient $b$ is nowhere zero by [F2] and the fiber-coordinate Jacobian. Data and fiber cutoffs are one near the base incidence point. Their transition pieces have $|z-q|\ge r>0$ after shrinking $x,v$; their integrals are $O(e^{-c\lambda})$ in every fixed object derivative by the finite-order distribution estimates and the Gaussian factor. Properness ensures the remaining relevant incidence portion is compact, so finitely many such estimates suffice. A fixed fiber cutoff can therefore be inserted without changing the formula except for these errors.

For $v\in V$ real there is a unique nearby real $t_0(v)$ with $z(t_0(v),X(v))=q$. At this point $\Psi_t=0$ by step 1.1. Put $D=D_xz$, $T=D_tz$, evaluated there. Its complex $t$ Hessian is $ H=B+iT^TT,\qquad B=-\partial_t^2(z\cdot p), $ where $B$ is real symmetric and $T$ is injective. This matrix is invertible: if $Hw=0$, the imaginary part of $w^*Hw$ is $|Tw|^2$, forcing $w=0$. Apply [F6] to the map retaining $(x,v)$ and replacing $t$ by $\Psi_t$; it gives a unique nearby complex critical point $t_c(x,v)$ for all nearby complex $x,v$. Shrink the original fiber neighborhood so it contains no other critical point: outside a small ball about $t_0$, continuity and the injectivity of the local coordinate chart preserve a positive lower bound for the phase gradient or for $|z-q|$. Define $\psi(x,v)=\Psi(t_c(x,v),x,v)$.

We prove its strict object positivity directly, rather than assume a positivity property of a formal stationary phase. At $(t_0,X(v),v)$ the full Hessian in $(t,x)$ is a complex symmetric matrix $ \mathcal H=\mathcal R+i\mathcal S,\qquad \mathcal S=[T\ D]^T[T\ D],\qquad \mathcal R=-\partial^2_{t,x}(z\cdot p). $ For a real object variation $h$, let $\tau$ be the complex solution of the stationary linearized equation $\mathcal H_{tt}\tau+\mathcal H_{tx}h=0$. Write $U=(\operatorname{Re}\tau,h)$ and $W=(\operatorname{Im}\tau,0)$. The real part of the stationary equation gives $(\mathcal R U)_t=(\mathcal S W)_t$. Therefore $ \operatorname{Im}\bigl((\tau,h)^T\mathcal H(\tau,h)\bigr) =U^T\mathcal S U-W^T\mathcal S W+2W^T\mathcal R U =|T\operatorname{Re}\tau+Dh|^2+|T\operatorname{Im}\tau|^2. $ This is precisely $\operatorname{Im}(h^T\psi_{xx}h)$ by differentiating the critical-point identity. If it is zero, injectivity of $T$ gives $\operatorname{Im}\tau=0$, and $T\tau+Dh=0$. The remaining stationary equation is $\mathcal R_{tt}\tau+\mathcal R_{tx}h=0$. These two equations say that $(\tau,h,\dot p=0)$ is a tangent variation of the conormal equations $(D_tz)^Tp=0$ and has $\dot z=\dot p=0$. By injectivity of $d\pi_L$ it is zero, so $h=0$. Compactness of the real unit sphere now gives a strictly positive lower bound for $\operatorname{Im}\psi_{xx}$, uniform for $v$ in a smaller compact neighborhood in $V$.

The critical-value and derivative identities are $ \psi(X(v),v)=-q\cdot p,\qquad \psi_x(X(v),v)=-D_xz(t_0,X(v))^Tp=-\Xi(v). $ The imaginary part and its first object derivative vanish there. Taylor's integral formula and the strict Hessian bound in step 3.1 therefore give $\operatorname{Im}\psi(x,v)\ge c|x-X(v)|^2$ for real $x,v$ nearby. This fixes the sign for the FBI pairing: the test function has derivative $-\Xi$, while the distributional covector detected is $+\Xi$.

Apply analytic stationary phase at the complex critical point in step 2.3. Its applicability here includes uniform contour and remainder estimates as follows. At the base real parameters the real $t$ contour has positive quadratic imaginary part $T^TT$; its outer boundary has a fixed positive imaginary margin by step 2.2. For nearby parameters move the interior contour through $t_c(x,v)$ using the holomorphic quadratic coordinates in [F4], keeping the boundary fixed. In those coordinates the contour remains a graph whose Gaussian real part is bounded below by a fixed positive quadratic form, by openness of positive definiteness. Interpolate to its linear tangent contour as in the Gaussian-contour proof; the cubic error is dominated after shrinking the fixed ball. Stokes deformation consequently has a fixed exponential boundary margin. Cauchy bounds for the amplitude and the inverse coordinate map are uniform on smaller complex parameter neighborhoods. Applying the normalized remainder in [F4] with $N=\lfloor\epsilon\lambda\rfloor$ gives $ K_\lambda=\lambda^{-d/2}e^{i\lambda\psi}A+E_\lambda. $ The leading coefficient of $A$ is $(2\pi)^{d/2}b(t_c(x,v),x)(\det(-i\Psi_{tt}(t_c(x,v),x,v)))^{-1/2}$ on the fixed analytic branch. At $x=X(v)$ the critical point is the real $t_0(v)$, where the density coefficient and Hessian determinant are nonzero; continuity and holomorphy therefore make this coefficient elliptic on a smaller neighborhood. Its coefficients have uniform factorial bounds. For real parameters $\operatorname{Im}\psi\ge0$, so normalized exponential errors also give absolute exponential errors. For fixed object derivatives take a smaller complex neighborhood where $|\operatorname{Im}\psi|$ is less than half the boundary/remainder margin and apply Cauchy; the cutoff transition pieces already have the corresponding finite-order real derivative bounds. Hence $E_\lambda=O(e^{-c_m\lambda})$ in every fixed object derivative as claimed.

Suppose the data Gaussian criterion holds. By [F5], its unit-direction formulation is equivalent to the Gaussian packet with $p$ in an open ball about the supplied nonzero data covector; positive radial frequency scaling only changes the exponential constant. Thus the data Gaussian pairings used in step 2.2 are uniformly exponentially small on an open parameter neighborhood. Pair the formula in step 5.1 with $u$; its finite order absorbs the errors. Multiply by $\lambda^{d/2}e^{i\lambda q\cdot p}$, whose modulus on real parameters is only polynomial. Pull back $v$ by the analytic section $v(Q,P)$ from step 2.1. The resulting object test phase $ \widetilde\psi(x,Q,P)=\psi(x,v(Q,P))+q(Q,P)\cdot p(Q,P) $ vanishes at $x=Q$, has derivative $-P$ there and imaginary part at least $c|x-Q|^2$. Its amplitude is elliptic by step 5.1. Thus [F5] converts this exponential estimate into the Gaussian criterion at $(x_0,\xi_0)$. All input support here is in the chosen local object neighborhood, and every tail and inverse error has been estimated before pairing with the distribution. This proves the local implication.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, say $u$ **vanishes on** an open $V\subseteq\Omega$ if its restriction to $V$ is zero. Let $Z$ be the union of all such open sets. Locality in [[thm-distributions-form-a-sheaf]] shows that $u|_Z=0$, since these sets cover $Z$ and all its restrictions are zero. Thus $Z$ is the largest vanishing open set. The **support** is the relatively closed set $\operatorname{supp}u=\Omega\setminus Z$.

In particular $\operatorname{supp}u=\varnothing$ if and only if $u=0$: emptiness gives $Z=\Omega$ and vanishing there, while the zero distribution vanishes everywhere. If a test $\varphi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$, its compact support is contained in $Z$, so $u(\varphi)=0$ by restriction. Consequently two tests agreeing on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$ have equal pairings with $u$, by applying this fact to their difference.

**Compactly supported** means that $\operatorname{supp}u$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Relative closedness in an arbitrary open domain is not by itself compactness or closedness in the ambient Euclidean space. On the empty domain support is empty. The union and locality argument require no selection of vanishing neighborhoods and no choice axiom.

For a smooth manifold $M^n$, with boundary allowed, the **density bundle** is $DM=\coprod_{p\in M}D(T_pM)$. In coordinates $x$, let $|dx|=|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ be the density taking value one on the coordinate frame. On overlaps,
$$|dy|=|\det D_x y|\,|dx|.$$
A smooth density is a section with smooth real coefficient in these frames. Its support is the closure of its nonzero locus. The absolute determinants are positive smooth transition functions and satisfy the cocycle identities by the chain rule. A countable atlas and [[thm-vector-bundle-construction-from-a-smooth-cocycle]] therefore give a smooth line bundle. For boundary charts the same gluing proof uses half-space product charts; smoothness of transitions follows from their local extensions, and Hausdorffness and second countability follow as for the supplied cocycle construction. The fibers are lines by [[prop-one-densities-form-a-one-dimensional-vector-space]]. When $n=0$ the empty frame trivializes $DM=M\times\mathbb R$.

For a smooth manifold $M$ and a point $p\in M$, the **cotangent space** at $p$ is the algebraic dual $T_p^*M:=(T_pM)^*$. The **cotangent bundle** is the disjoint union
$$ T^*M:=\bigsqcup_{p\in M} T_p^*M. $$

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Every compactly supported distribution $v\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ has a
unique extension $\widetilde v\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.  Restricting
$\widetilde v$ to $\mathcal D$ recovers $v$.  No choice axiom is required.

Give $C^\infty(\Omega)$ the topology generated by $q_{K,m}(f)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $m\ge0$. A compactly supported distribution $u$ has a unique continuous complex-linear extension to this space, given by
$$\widetilde u(f)=u(\chi f),$$
where $\chi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is any cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}u$. The result is independent of $\chi$. The extension vanishes on every smooth function zero near the support. No Hahn–Banach or choice axiom is needed.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be a smooth submersion at $p\in M$. Then there are charts
near $p$ and $F(p)$ in which the coordinate representative of $F$ is

$$ (u,v)\longmapsto u $$

near the distinguished point.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: In submersion coordinates $(x,v)$, a compactly supported test density on $Y$ is $\psi(x,v)|dx\,dv|$. Its fiber integral is $\widetilde\psi(x)=\int\psi(x,v)|dv|$. The integrand has compact support, so differentiation under the integral gives a smooth function; its support lies in the compact projection of $\operatorname{supp}\psi$. Thus $\widetilde\psi(x)|dx|$ is a test density and transposing this operation defines $p^*u$.

If $q$ is proper on $\operatorname{supp}V$ and $K$ is compact in $M$, then $Q_K=q^{-1}(K)\cap\operatorname{supp}V$ is compact. Choose one smooth cutoff $\beta_K$ equal to one near $Q_K$. For every test function $\varphi$ supported in $K$, define $\langle q_*V,\varphi\rangle=\langle V,\beta_K(\varphi\circ q)\rangle$. If another cutoff is used, the difference of the two test functions vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}V$: it vanishes near $Q_K$ because both cutoffs equal one there, and away from $Q_K$ either $V$ vanishes or $\varphi\circ q=0$. Hence [F4] gives the same pairing. The chain and product rules bound every fixed-support seminorm of $\beta_K(\varphi\circ q)$ by finitely many fixed-support seminorms of $\varphi$, so continuity of $V$ proves continuity of $q_*V$. A finite cover by coordinate balls and [F12] supplies $\beta_K$. Multiplication by a smooth density is defined by the stated transpose formula, so the typed pushforward is well-defined.

In coordinates where $Z=\{t=0\}$, the incidence functional is integration of the restricted test function against $\omega_Z$. Under a change of coordinates on $Z$, the coefficient of $\omega_Z$ transforms by the absolute tangential Jacobian [F5]. Thus the functional is independent of the defining chart.

A covector annihilating $T_zZ$ transforms by the inverse transpose rule [F6], so $N^*Z$ and $C_Z$ are coordinate independent. If a conormal has the form $(\eta,0)$, it annihilates the image of $d\pi_G:T_{(g,x)}Z\to T_gG$, which is all of $T_gG$ because $\pi_G$ is a submersion; therefore $\eta=0$. Applying the same argument to $\pi_X$ shows that $(0,\xi)$ can only be zero.

On overlapping submersion charts, the full absolute Jacobian factors into the base Jacobian and the fiber-density quotient. The fiber integral therefore transforms as a base density. This proves that the transposed functional in step 1.1 is chart independent.

Let $\varphi$ be any compactly supported test density on $M$; the zero test is immediate. Its support $K$ is compact. Cover $K$ by finitely many smaller coordinate balls $B_i$ whose closures lie in coordinate balls $U_i$. Using [F12] in each chart, choose $\beta_i$ supported in $U_i$ and equal to one on $B_i$, and put $\sigma=\sum_i\beta_i$. Then $\sigma>0$ on a neighborhood of $K$. A second finite cover by coordinate balls and [F12] gives a compactly supported smooth $\theta$ in $\{\sigma>0\}$ equal to one near $K$. Define $\chi_i=\theta\beta_i/\sigma$ on $\{\sigma>0\}$ and extend by zero outside. Each $\chi_i$ is smooth and compactly supported in $U_i$, and $\sum_i\chi_i=\theta$. Hence $u(\varphi)=\sum_i u(\chi_i\varphi)$, since $\theta=1$ near $K$. Each term is a chartwise pairing with a compactly supported Euclidean distribution, so [F9] and [F10] give its tempered and smooth-function realizations. The finite sum therefore recovers the original functional and its packet pairings, without assuming $\operatorname{supp}u$ compact or choosing global coordinates.
